lectures.name: Intro to Diabetes
lectures.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
lectures.framing: Both types are diagnosed by the same glucose thresholds — what separates them is the mechanism producing the hyperglycemia: absolute autoimmune insulin deficiency vs. a spectrum of insulin resistance and relative deficiency.
lectures.keypoints: the alpha cells are spared in T1DM — the lesion is beta-cell specific. Autoantibody count, not presence, is what carries risk (1 = background risk, 3 = 40% in five years). GAD is the specific marker. Monozygotic concordance is higher in T2DM (90%) than T1DM (50%) — the counterintuitive fact worth remembering. And the octet explains why T2DM needs combination therapy: each drug class corrects a different defect.

lectures.name: Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes
lectures.title: Approach to New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes
lectures.framing: The whole diagnosis turns on one question: are symptoms present? If yes, a single abnormal glucose is sufficient — do not delay treatment for a confirmatory test.
lectures.keypoints: symptoms present → one abnormal glucose diagnoses diabetes; no symptoms → two are needed. The DCCT trial logic underlies everything here — intensive insulin therapy ↓ A1c and ↓ long-term microvascular complications but ↑ hypoglycemia, a trade-off now partly offset by pumps and CGM. Glucose gel works through buccal mucosa, so it can be given when swallowing is unsafe.

blocks.html: Workup skeleton

• Hx — the three classic early symptoms nearly every patient has: polyuria (including nocturia / new bed-wetting), excessive thirst, weight loss despite unchanged or ↑ appetite. Then screen for late/severe features: vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, hyperventilation, fatigue, ↓ level of consciousness.
  • PEx — hydration status, weight loss, level of consciousness, Kussmaul breathing, acetone breath.
  • Ix — random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1, urine dipstick for glucose and ketones, serum C-peptide (is she making any insulin?), ABG if DKA suspected. ⚠ FPG and A1c are usually unnecessary here — the diagnosis is already clear.
  • Tx — insulin + structured education; treat DKA emergently if present.
  • Follow-up — annual urinalysis for albuminuria (diabetic nephropathy screening).

rows: ≥ 11.1 mmol/L ← the one that matters acutely

blocks.lead: Management — the four education pillars (delivered by a multidisciplinary team: dietician, social worker, diabetes nurse educator)

blocks.html: Treatment: give ~15 g of fast-acting sugar — glucose tablet or juice · glucose gel (absorbed rapidly across buccal mucosa) · glucagon (IM, SC or intranasal) · IV dextrose. Prevention: treat early symptoms promptly, monitor regularly, adjust insulin before and after exercise, adhere to the meal plan.

lectures.name: Pharmacology of Insulin
lectures.title: Insulin Preparations
lectures.framing: Choose a preparation based on what the insulin is covering — a meal (bolus) or the fasting state (basal). Onset and duration are set by one thing: how fast monomers dissociate from the hexamer, since insulin binds its receptor only as a monomer. Anything that stabilizes the hexamer (zinc, protamine, self-aggregation, albumin binding) → slower onset, longer duration.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Analogues are NOT more effective at lowering HbA1c than human insulin — they are safer and more convenient (faster onset, better postprandial match, lower variability, less nocturnal hypoglycemia). Only regular insulin can be given IV. Basal insulins must never be used in pumps, and most basal insulins must not be mixed with another insulin before injection. Insulin does not interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other drugs — but drugs that alter glucose metabolism (e.g. steroids ↑ hepatic glucose production) change how well it works. Exogenous insulin is imperfect because physiological secretion is glucose-dependent, and that fine-tuning is lost.

lectures.name: Clinically Useful Endocrine Principles
lectures.framing: p# Overview chart: Approach to a Suspected Endocrine Problem
lectures.keypoints: the suppression/stimulation pairing is the single most testable idea here — excess is tested by trying to turn it off, deficiency by trying to turn it on. primary adrenal insufficiency loses both cortisol AND aldosterone, which is what separates it from central causes. A benign mass can still be clinically important through pure mass effect. And always ask whether an exogenous hormone explains the picture before working up the gland.

blocks.html: Every endocrine problem sorts into structural (a mass) or functional (too much or too little hormone) — and both can be present at once. The sorting question determines the entire workup.

blocks.lead: Four questions to ask of any functional problem: What does the hormone do? · What feedback loops could be affected? · Is the problem in the gland itself (primary) or somewhere else (secondary / tertiary / central)? · Can this be explained by an exogenous source of hormone?

blocks.lead: Dynamic testing — the logic is always the mirror of the problem. Suspect excess → suppress. Suspect deficiency → stimulate.

blocks.html: Orientation: hormones serve four jobs — reproduction (estradiol, testosterone, prolactin) · growth and development (growth hormone, sex steroids) · maintaining the internal environment (triiodothyronine, ADH, PTH) · making, storing and using energy (insulin, glucagon, cortisol). By distance to target: autocrine = the cell itself · paracrine = a nearby cell · endocrine = distant, reached via the bloodstream.

lectures.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology
lectures.title: Diagnosing T2DM and the Grey Zone
lectures.framing: T1DM and T2DM share identical diagnostic thresholds — so the diagnostic work is (1) crossing the threshold, (2) deciding how many measurements you need, and (3) working out which type you are looking at.
lectures.keypoints: symptomatic → one measurement; asymptomatic → two. Do not diagnose during acute illness (MI, sepsis, steroids) — suspect, then confirm on recovery. C-peptide and anti-GAD move in opposite directions between the two types: low C-peptide + high anti-GAD = T1DM. >90% of all diabetes is Type 2; 589M adults live with diabetes worldwide (~1 in 9), ~43% of them undiagnosed, and ~30% of Canadians have diabetes or prediabetes. Finally — a T2DM diagnosis is not necessarily permanent: weight loss, activity and diet can return glucose below the diabetic range, though it can recur, so keep checking a few times a year.

blocks.html: Risk factors. Genetic: mostly polygenic — 90% monozygotic twin concordance, 40% have an affected parent, 5–10% ↑ lifetime risk with a 1st-degree relative. Environmental: obesogenic foods (low fibre, high fat, high simple sugars), "portion creep", inactivity. Populations at particular risk: South and East Asian, Hispanic, Indigenous, African American, and women with previous gestational diabetes.

lectures.name: Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes
lectures.title: Complications of Diabetes
lectures.framing: The acute emergencies separate on one variable: is there enough insulin to suppress lipolysis? Enough → no ketones → HHS. Not enough → ketogenesis → DKA.
lectures.keypoints: abdominal pain and vomiting = DKA, not HHS. Hours = DKA, days = HHS. T1DM = DKA, older T2DM = HHS. SGLT2 inhibitors can precipitate DKA — and appear again in the sick-day rules as a drug to stop. Potassium falls with treatment, not before it. Proprioception goes early in peripheral neuropathy, and feet are affected before hands because of nerve length.

blocks.title: The two traps that kill
blocks.html:
① Potassium. Total body K⁺ is depleted even when the initial serum potassium looks normal — in DKA, low insulin has driven K⁺ extracellularly. Once you give fluid and insulin, K⁺ shifts back intracellularly and falls sharply, causing arrhythmias and death. K⁺ replacement is often required during treatment.

② Glucose falling too fast. IV fluids and insulin will drop glucose. Add dextrose to the fluids so insulin can keep running until the dehydration — and in DKA the acidosis — is corrected.

lectures.framing: Choose an agent based on which step of glucose metabolism is being manipulated, then narrow by hypoglycemia risk, effect on weight, and organ function!
lectures.keypoints: GLP-1RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors are the agents with proven cardiovascular benefit — pick one in a patient with CV disease. Only the secretagogues (SUs, meglitinides) carry meaningful hypoglycemia risk, because they release insulin independent of glucose level; the incretins do not, because their secretion is glucose-dependent. Weight gain: TZDs, SUs, meglitinides. Weight loss: GLP-1RAs, SGLT2i, (metformin). Two classes stop at eGFR < 30: metformin (lactic acidosis) and SGLT2 inhibitors (no filtered glucose to block).

lectures.name: Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes
lectures.title: Glycemic Goals of Care
lectures.framing: The target is never a single number — it is a negotiation between preventing long-term complications and avoiding hypoglycemia now. Tight control buys microvascular benefit; severe hypoglycemia carries ↑ mortality.
lectures.keypoints: severity of hypoglycemia is defined by whether the patient can treat it themselves — not by the glucose number. A1c is the best-validated marker of control but lags, so it never replaces glucose readings when you are actively changing therapy. CGM measures interstitial, not blood, glucose. Tight control helps microvascular outcomes most; the macrovascular gain is smaller and slower — and in T2DM, blood pressure control is what drives CV risk down.

lectures.name: Introduction to Obesity
lectures.title: Obesity — Assessment and Management
lectures.framing: Obesity is a complex, progressive, relapsing chronic disease — abnormal or excessive body fat that impairs health. BMI alone does not predict adiposity-related complications; stage the impact, not just the number.
lectures.keypoints: tirzepatide (dual GLP-1/GIP) beats semaglutide beats naltrexone-bupropion for weight loss. The most serious post-bariatric deficiency is thiamine — give it before any glucose or you precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy. The BMI cut-off drops to 25 for South and East Asian patients. EOSS stages the functional impact, which is what determines bariatric referral — not BMI alone. Ghrelin is the only fasting/hunger hormone here; everything else in the list promotes satiety. The pharmacotherapy stopping rule is 5% at 12 weeks. Gastric banding is explicitly not recommended. And 20% of Canadians have obesity, with the socioeconomic gradient running opposite ways by sex — ↓ SES means ↑ obesity in women, ↓ in men.

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["BMI ≥ 30 — or ≥ 25 in South/East Asian patients"] --> B["Add waist circumference
BMI alone is insufficient"] B --> C["ASK permission to discuss weight"] C --> D["ASSESS: EOSS stage + the 4 M's
rule out secondary causes"] D --> E["ADVISE: health and wellness, not a number"] E --> F["AGREE: SMART goals
0.5–1.0 kg/week, 5–10% over 6–12 months"] F --> G["ASSIST: barriers, referrals, follow-up"] D --> H{"Eligible for escalation?"} H -->|"BMI ≥ 30, or ≥ 27 with complications"| I["Pharmacotherapy"] H -->|"BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with complications,
or ≥ 30 with poorly controlled T2DM"| J["Bariatric surgery"]

blocks.lead: Defining it — thresholds are ethnicity-specific, because BMI and waist circumference do not account for body frame, musculature, or propensity for visceral adiposity.

blocks.html: ⚠ South and East Asian individuals develop visceral adiposity and obesity-related disease at a lower BMI — this is why the cut-off moves.

blocks.lead: Complications — the 4 M's. Use this as the assessment checklist, not a list to memorise loosely.
rows: Cognition · depression · ADHD · addiction · psychosis · eating disorders · trauma · insomnia
sleep apnea · osteoarthritis · chronic pain · GERD · incontinence · venous thromboembolism · intertrigo · plantar fasciitis
T2DM · dyslipidemia · essential hypertension · gout · fatty liver · gallstones · PCOS · cancer
Education · employment · income · insurance · benefits · disability · weight loss programs · bariatric supplies

blocks.lead: Pathophysiology — far more than energy in vs. energy out. 60–70% of BMI is genetically determined. Early-life events matter (maternal starvation in pregnancy predisposes offspring to obesity). The hypothalamus (homeostasis), mesolimbic system (pleasure) and frontal lobe (executive control) jointly drive food-seeking: dopamine = wanting food, opioids = liking food.
rows: ghrelin — made in the stomach, ↑ hunger and food intake

insulin, amylin — pancreas
GLP-1, CCK, peptide YY — intestines
leptin, adiponectin — adipose tissue

rows: Be non-judgemental · explore readiness for change · use motivational interviewing
Stage the disease and find root causes

EOSS stage · BMI + WC if BMI ≥ 25 · the 4 M's
Hx weight history, contributors, rule out hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, medications, genetic disorders, cultural and family factors, diet and exercise history
PEx BMI, WC, blood pressure, acanthosis, hirsutism, Cushingoid features
Labs HbA1c, lipid panel, serum TSH, ALT
⭐ The goal is health and wellness, not a number. First goal may simply be stabilising weight; behavioural change yields 3–5%

Referrals (e.g. cardiology before an exercise plan) · contingency plans for travel · financial reality — dieticians are often out of pocket

blocks.lead: Management — two foundations, three pillars
rows: Personalized; refer to a registered dietician, especially with celiac disease or IBD
30–60 min most days, moderate–vigorous. Yields small weight/fat loss but improves cardiometabolic parameters and is key to maintaining loss
Behaviour modification · manage sleep, stress, time · CBT and/or ACT

⭐ Efficacy order: tirzepatide (GLP-1/GIP) > semaglutide (GLP-1) > naltrexone-bupropion; orlistat rarely used
⭐ Should achieve ≥ 5% weight loss after 12 weeks at maximally tolerated dose — if not, change agent. Adjunct to lifestyle, but likely lifelong
BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with complications, or ⭐ ≥ 30 with poorly controlled T2DM

25–30% weight loss; ↓ long-term mortality. sleeve gastrectomy · Roux-en-Y gastric bypass · biliopancreatic diversion ± duodenal switch · laparoscopic gastric banding no longer performed
⭐ Post-op: thiamine before glucose — always

blocks.title: Bias, stigma and the clinic itself
blocks.html: 56% of patients have already attempted weight loss two or more times — assume effort, not inaction. Chairs, exam tables, bathrooms and scales must accommodate the patient. Place the scale in a private area, and do not announce weight unless they ask to hear it.

lectures.name: Prevention of Complications of Diabetes
lectures.title: Preventing the Complications of Diabetes
lectures.framing: Three numbers drive prevention — A1c, blood pressure, and LDL — and each has its own first-line drug and its own set of complications it prevents. Glycemic control alone is not enough: it barely moves macrovascular risk.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Glycemic control prevents microvascular disease; blood pressure control is what prevents macrovascular disease in T2DM. ACEi/ARB are given for nephropathy even in patients without hypertension (see 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes). Feet are examined daily at home and at every clinic visit — the monofilament test detects the loss of protective sensation before ulceration. The > 15 years of diabetes clause matters: a 35-year-old diagnosed at 18 qualifies for a statin.

rows: ≤ 7% (see 08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes)

blocks.lead: What the trials actually showed — DCCT 1993 for T1DM, UKPDS 1998 for T2DM. Better glycemic control and more intensive regimens produced:
rows: ⭐ NO effect from glycemic control — but ↓ blood pressure ↓ CVD risk in T2DM
⚠ ↑ risk — the cost of intensive control

blocks.lead: Cardiovascular prevention — the age and duration triggers are the testable part.
rows:
≥ 30 yrs AND DM > 15 years → statin
≥ 40 yrs → statin
> 55 yrs AND other CAD risk factors (proteinuria, retinopathy, LVH) → ACEi or ARB IN ADDITION to a statin

blocks.html: Drug classes with benefit beyond glucose: SGLT2 inhibitors → cardiovascular AND renal protection. incretin agents → cardiovascular protection.

blocks.lead: Lifestyle and in-clinic monitoring
rows: Home monitoring of glucose AND blood pressure
↓ risk of MI, stroke, PAD, and possibly retinopathy
If vision impaired — ask a family member, or refer to chiropody; ensure comfortable shoes
Inspect for calluses and ulcers · assess pedal pulses · monofilament exam

blocks.lead: At the moment of diagnosis — refer early. Dietician (dietary change to ↓ complication risk) · diabetes nurse educator (sugar testing, what to do when low or sick) · optometrist (yearly).
rows: All T1DM, and T2DM patients who are very symptomatic (polydipsia, polyuria, yeast infections, weight loss, malaise)
T2DM without many symptoms and no liver or renal concerns

lectures.name: Pregnancy and Diabetes
lectures.title: Diabetes in Pregnancy
lectures.framing: The single discriminating question is when the hyperglycemia starts. Pre-existing DM is present during organogenesis (weeks 3–16) → congenital malformations. GDM appears at 24–28 weeks, after organogenesis → NO congenital malformations, but the same fetal morbidities.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ GDM does not cause congenital malformations; pre-existing DM does — because of when the hyperglycemia occurs relative to organogenesis. Insulin needs FALL in trimester 1 and after delivery, and RISE steeply in trimester 3. Glyburide crosses the placenta; insulin does not. ACEi/ARBs are contraindicated — use beta-blockers or CCBs. Retinopathy that worsens in pregnancy usually settles after delivery without permanent damage, but screen pre-conception, during, and within the first postpartum year. Fetal death risk is low (0.6–4.8%) — malformation risk is the greater concern.

lectures.name: Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes
lectures.title: Preventing Type 2 Diabetes
lectures.framing: The target population is the grey zone — prediabetes, IFG and IGT (see 05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology). ⭐ No medication is approved in Canada for preventing diabetes — everything below is evidence, not indication.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Lifestyle beats metformin, 58% vs 31% — the single most testable number in this lecture. TZDs have the biggest drug effect (~70%) but the side effect profile that stops you using them. Acarbose's benefit disappears on discontinuation, unlike the durable effect of weight loss. Bariatric surgery is the most effective and still not first line — effectiveness and appropriateness are different questions. And nothing here is actually approved for prevention in Canada.

rows: ⭐ Low-fat, low-calorie diet + 150 min activity per week
31% — roughly half the benefit of lifestyle
⭐ More effective in the younger (< 60 yrs), the obese (BMI > 35), and women with previous GDM
⚠ Limited by adverse effects: peripheral edema, heart failure, osteoporosis and ↑ fractures
Assessed within obesity effectiveness studies; approved for weight loss, not prevention
⚠ NOT first line for prevention — cost and procedural risk

lectures.name: Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)
lectures.title: Choosing an Antihyperglycemic — Case Analysis
lectures.framing: Every case runs the same four-part analysis: effectiveness → safety → additional benefits → suitability. The drug is chosen by the patient's characteristics, not the A1c alone.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Sulfonylurea secondary failure means the next drug must not be another secretagogue. Linagliptin is the DPP-4 inhibitor that needs no renal adjustment. SGLT2 inhibitors cause GU infections and volume depletion — and cause DKA at normal glucose. AGIs are contraindicated in IBS and IBD. When insulin requirements exceed anything plausible, stop escalating and look for a receptor-level cause.

rows: How much do I need to drop?

High: insulin, metformin, GLP-1 analogues, SUs, TZDs
Moderate: DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, AGIs
Does the patient need to lose weight — or are they already cachectic?
Loss: GLP-1 RA, SGLT2i · Gain: SU, TZD, insulin
⭐ Do they live alone, drive, eat irregularly, or fear hypos?
Cost · injection vs oral · dosing frequency · adherence

blocks.lead: The four cases — each teaches one mechanism.
rows:
1 — Hyperglycemia refractory to insulin
46 F, BMI 45.6 → 16.9, A1c 14%, insulin > 50 units/kg/day
Cachexia with extreme insulin requirement; acromegaly-like facies, extensive acanthosis nigricans, skin tags, vitiligo; UTI on empagliflozin; H. pylori triple therapy
Severe insulin resistance syndrome — when escalating insulin fails, the problem is at the receptor, not the dose
Ask what explains resistance this extreme; note SGLT2 inhibitors → glucosuria → GU infection, and that SU + TZD + insulin stack weight gain and hypoglycemia

2 — Samuel, 47 M, A1c 8.3%
dyslipidemia, +12 lb, forgets BID metformin, travels constantly, IBS
Poor adherence to twice-daily dosing · needs weight loss · eats at consistent times
Favour once-weekly GLP-1RAs or once-daily agents with weight loss; ⛔ AGIs are contraindicated in IBS and are t.i.d.
3 — Nancy, 62 F, A1c 7.1% → 7.9% on max metformin + gliclazide, +5 lb, unemployed, refuses needles, fears hypoglycemia, eats irregularly
Wants: glycemic control · weight loss · low hypoglycemia risk · affordable · oral
⭐ Sulfonylurea secondary failure — the K⁺/ATP channel mechanism desensitizes over time
Do not swap to another secretagogue (glyburide or repaglinide share the mechanism); needs an agent with no hypoglycemia risk, oral, affordable

4 — Albert, 72 M, ICU with AKI and shock
on canagliflozin + hydrochlorothiazide + valsartan; 18 months of falls from postural hypotension
Triple volume-depleting combination; foot swelling, ↓ urine output, nausea, dyspnea
SGLT2i → glucosuria → osmotic diuresis → volume depletion → prerenal AKI; plus ⭐ euglycemic DKA
Recognise that the falls were the warning sign; hold the SGLT2 inhibitor and diuretic; check ketones regardless of glucose

blocks.title: Euglycemic DKA — the SGLT2 inhibitor trap
blocks.html: DKA can occur with a near-normal blood glucose, because urinary glucose loss blunts the hyperglycemia you would normally use as your trigger to test. ⭐ Suspect it in any unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor and check ketones regardless of the glucose reading.

blocks.lead: Antihyperglycemics and renal function (Shah BR et al. Can J Diabetes 2024;48:415-424) — principles, not numbers:
rows: Stepwise dose reduction, then avoid at the lowest ranges
⭐ Glyburide is avoided relatively early; gliclazide, glimepiride and repaglinide tolerate moderate impairment better
Most need dose reduction — ⭐ EXCEPT linagliptin, which needs none (non-renal clearance)
Typically "do not initiate, but may continue" below a threshold
⭐ Cardiorenal benefits persist even where glucose-lowering efficacy falls off — which is why an SGLT2 inhibitor may be continued in CKD for reasons other than glycemic control
